There is absolutely no reason to avoid buying this on sale.  In it's current state, it's worth $30-$40 bucks.  I don't argue that it won't be worth $60 one day, either, but considering how this game released, and considering what was promised and not delivered initially, I can see the 'why' to the inital uproar in negative reviews.  Also with very few sales and the persistent $60 price tag, I can see why negative reviews would continue to linger on, even up until now.  But now, for any negative reviews to sound like they did a year ago, would be unacceptable.  The game was not released in a fashion that it was promised it would be:  shame on you Hello Games.  You continued to ask $60 for it:  also, slight shaming from me because that ultimately held off my purchase until the summer sale of 2017.  And in that course of time not only did I get a cheaper copy of the game, but there were at least 2 major updates that occurred during my absence of owning NMS.   So to have started the game a month ago, I can leave no other review than an absolutely positive one.  Buy this game at what price you can afford.  Chill out, and relax.  But also be prepared for change, because I don't think they are finished with this game yet.  And to Hello Games, Thank You.  For not giving up, and making it better.  It makes up for releasing it the way you did.  I can't wait to try out today's update.  I doubt I'll be coming back to change my recommendation for No Man's Sky.  Update:  I called it.  It's worth $60 now, and I wouldn't be sad if I waited until now to buy it for full price.  If you're still on the fence, grab it on sale.  Nothing wrong with that at all.  But this company deserves you to come back if you left in the past and/or refunded.  And for the newcomers....you have no idea what you didn't miss out on in the beginning, but to see the evolution of this game in the form of several free, major updates since release........I mean...I'm blown away.  Again, thank you team Hello Games.  If there was ever a shining star at the end of a dark tunnel of abandonment, it's this team of devs.  Others need to follow suit.  Immediately.  That is all.

When No Man's Sky came out about a year ago, it was pretty ♥♥♥♥. It was basically a $60 sight seeing game that was fun for about 2 hours before you finally got bored and uninstalled the game.  Well one year later, and that statement above couldn't be further from the truth. I strongly believe that No Man's Sky is now the game that we were promised it would be, and the devs show no sign of stopping there. The once boring and linear storyline that lasted 30 minutes is now a diverse storyline that branches off into different stories, that you can explore and follow however you want. 12 hours in and I'm still nowhere near done with the story. You now no longer have to just fly around aimlessly with your tiny ship, you can trade ships or find ships at crashsites and repair them, you can buy your own capital freightership, you can make your own base and recruit a crew, there are space battles, pirates, side missions, etc. What I'm trying to say here is that a LOT has changed, if you haven't tried NMS yet or bought it originally but just uninstalled it, give it a chance, you will be amazed how far it has come.

After the mess that was the launch of No Man's Sky I think it deserved the response it received. We were promised many things, many of the things we were promised were not in the game we paid $60 for. Hello Games (especially Sean Murray) have been dragged through the mud since release. They could have taken every single cent from the huge amount of sales the game made and ran, but THEY didn't. From the rumors of Hello Games offices being abandoned to the MONTHS of silence from Hello Games . They've come through, and from my understanding of Sean's GDC talk they simply ran out of money. NMS is an incredibly ambitious title for such a small team to create. I won't excuse their handling of the situation but in reality, even if they had told everyone that they ran out of money there would have been an uproar. Not nearly as big but none the less...an uproar.   I bought this game, I told my friends to pre-order. Non of us refunded it as we all had spent too long to be in the window but while we were stuck with this game we accepted what it was and that we were essentially out $60. Then, the first update came. It wasn't much but it was a glimmer of hope that Hello Games cared enough about this game to at least salvage it. Each subsequent update made that glimmer bright and brighter. With Atlas Rises I don't think anyone can logically question that Hello Games at least has the integrity to push through this dark, and dreary year they've had to see this passion project through. I've put at least 15hrs in since the Atlas Rises update and I've barely scratched the surface of what this update has brought.   Is it worth $60? Did the version we were shown back before release look worth $60? If so then I would say yes. It is now 96% of the way towards being the game we were shown. (still no giant sand worms Sean!) The game we all fell in love with, the game we all spent our money on. The game Sean Murray teased and teased only to let us down for reasons we may never have the complete answers to. It's right there, in front of us all now. It's been a year since the implosion of the hype trains core. We've had time to settle, Hello Games has been rebuilding and damn it. They've rebuilt.

CAVEAT: I waited and started the game after 1.33, which is a whole new game from version 1.0.  This game is simply incredible! This is above and beyond what I had wanted out of ANY space exploration game, and certainly 100x better than the initial release version. I had a day off and I put 9 hours into the game in one day (and that was all on the starting planet, after I received my first spaceship, and found a crashed/damaged Hauler which I proceeded to fix-up).   Right now, I have a cumulative of 13.3 hours into the experience, and I don't have a vast majority of the content or story unlocked. I am aware of the state the game came-out in and what was missing, but after reading the patch notes of the last 3 patches (really should be referred to as MASSIVE expansions!... did I mention they were free?!), the game is now a LOT deeper than it was.   I really wanted to get this game on pre-order, but my gut told me it may not live-up to the hype... and it didn't. After a MASSIVE over-haul, and when it was on sale for 66% off, it was a no-brainer for me to get this thing finally.  One of the early complaints I saw were about how people got bored with the game and just blazed through the (at the time) limited story narrative with nothing to achieve... I started my first game in Survival mode. I highly recommend it, as it is exactly as advertised. Death came early to me while I was learning that I could not breath the toxic atmosphere of my first planet and that I had to gather resources, dart from cave to cave, and look for bases and other points of interest rather than just running willy-nilly to my main objective and getting off the planet.  There were TONS of Points of Interest on my starting planet, and they were a pleasure to look for. Resources were available, but definitely scarce, so survival definitely played a huge part in the exploration even after getting a ridiculously great Class A Multitool by pure random chance from one of the aliens I encountered early-on. Sure, you could fly anywhere quickly, but would you have access to enough Plutonium to power your thrusters to get up in the air again? Most of the time the answer was 'no'... I had to venture through caves and explore minutes away from my spacecraft to gather what I needed. The wildlife was passive (thankfully), but the atmosphere was always choking me.  Going off planet to a hot moon for the first time was even more abusive (in a great way)... I was greeted by a fast howling creature which resulted in at least 3 deaths until I figured-out what the heck it was... and it was mean... and made me jump when I heard the scurrying sounds through my surround sound in the middle of the night. I would jump on top of my ship as soon as I would land just to scout the surroundings. It was a legit Aliens-type feeling, especially since the small moon was densely populated with other wild life which was constantly being spooked... and for good reason with that six-legged bas**** running around! Resources were even scarcer than on my first planet, and after several reloads (after I figured-out that I could reload saves >_<!), I managed to escape with next to no resources (which I felt were adequately stock-piled from the first planet), 1 health unit, literally drained Life Support, and no shields/resistance to the elements.  Next planet was in the new system and it was a beautiful Paradise planet with vast oceans and green islands... except it was crawling with ANGRY Sentinels that apparently destroyed all life... I was forced to run multiple times. Ultimately learned how to deal with them after a couple of near-deaths, and started farming as many as I could from a different location to net me some great loot. I have no idea how to survive going back to the central point crawling with Sentinels on this planet, but I gladly try! :)  I am pleased to announce that in Survival Mode, the game difficulty being 'too easy' is no longer an issue. There are multiple ways of farming money, and everything can kill you, but you always have a chance once you learn the basics. The game is difficult, but not brutal. I got a feeling of playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. in space on more than a few occasions as I explored abandoned buildings, way points, and crash sites... it was wonderful!  I saw what the graphics looked like before, and I have to say that they look incredible at 1440p and a 980ti now. I have the FPS cap set to 60fps with VSYNC on, and I feel like the game is smooth but may occasionally dip, as judged by moments when it the game runs like butter. It is a minor note, as the game plays very consistently, and I can't tell if maybe the frame drops are in my head or not.  I did find a base with an Architect I could claim on the first planet, but have so far decided not to build my first base prior to unlocking some more Blueprints and greater access to credits and resources. So yeah, I have not even touched on one of the largest aspects of the game, not to mention the freighters! All I know is that I landed on the first Class C Freighter I saw, and the captain offered to sell it to me for 192 million credits... I had about 200K at the time.  So at this point I am GREATLY looking forward to spending more time with this game, while my girlfriend is terrified that I won't see here ever again... well, for at least the next 100 hours or so. ;)  Pros: - Great graphics - Fairly easy to figure everything out, so the learning curve is not particularly steep... if you know how to play FPS games and may have played a Survival-type game, you will probably do well. - Really great Survival Mode, which should be the default in my opinion - Tons to explore - Vastly improved planet types and creatures over the original - New progression system - Interesting economy mechanics - Really fun exponential growth model that REALLY lets you feel like you are starting from nothing and growing into a force to be reckoned with - Faction system that gives you additional unlocks - Great spaceship variety (in terms of visuals, however I have seen pretty interesting stat and slot combinations also... this is always going to be subjective, though) - Sound design gives weapons weight and startling moments when something sneaks-up on you (if you have surround sound) - There are vehicles now, too?! O_O - Plans for even more content, while the current build is already amazing!  Cons: - Not a lot of details on how to actually survive when you first start... I had no idea caves could protect me from toxic gas, which is the exact opposite of what I would personally expect (greater gas in cave pockets, not less o_O... I can live with it, though). - No explanation of the Quick Menu and all of the cool things you can do with it... pretty easy to use and figure-out at least. - Still some optimization work may help performance on older machines and fix the odd crash (I only had 1 when I loaded a prior save for the first time), but still highly playable.  Conclusion: The game has evolved greatly from its initial release, and this is exactly the type of game I wanted for the longest time. It seems to do things in an simpler/easier way than games like Elite Dangerous, but at the same time it does a lot of things better, and maybe a handful of things worse. It's a must buy for any lovers of space and survival genres, especially if you are looking for a great single-player experience as opposed to having to be surrounded by people in typically MMO's. You are truly a lost traveler and it feels like it in this world. I feel like it's finally worth full price, but it's a complete steal if you get it on sale! Two thumbs up! :)

What a rollercoaster this game is.  I pre-ordered, and felt absolutely cheated when the initial release came. We've all read the news stories and seen the enraged posts online -- the lying, the deceptive claims, the huge tracts of missing content. Many developers would have taken a hit like that and sunk their game in the deepest hole they could find.  Instead, the devs spent a year making update after update, all free, slowly struggling to live up to the grandiose claims they'd made in the first place. It's still not as ideal as actually releasing the game as promised in the first place, but now, finally, No Man's Sky feels something like an actual game. With some faint glimmers of story and worldbuilding wrapped around the gorgeous procedural galaxies, it's able to hold itself together -- if only just.  It's still not worth the full price, but I would eagerly suggest grabbing it on sale. It's beautiful, the music is lovely, the takeoff-to-orbit flight has zero loading screens, and every update has improved the game. There's not much story or ultimate goal to speak of, but it's not about rescuing a space princess. It's just about seeing what's out there. And now, at last, the answer is "something".  EDIT:  TL;DR / Summary -- They lied and called an Early Access game a polished blockbuster, but after tons of updates and two DLC Expansion sized upgrades, the game is juuuuust about worth buying on sale, if only for some truly beautiful procedural vistas.

In short - the thousands of existing reviews aren't wrong. Knowing the reputation it had, I still had some interest in No Man's Sky and I finally got NMS on sale around the time of the 1.3 update. Right off the bat the game would crash at the loading screen. I thought maybe it was a graphics or configuration setting. Then I noticed you aren't given the option to make any configuration changes... There's no main menu, only a difficulty select screen. So I never would have known if that was the problem. Having to load the game before you can change graphics settings? That's a horrible design choice. After a quick internet search I found out that NMS has a known issue with my specific series of AMD graphics... So, in my frustration and research I found that NMS allows mods, and THANK THE INTERNET GODS FOR NOMANSSKYMODS dot COM!!!! One of the top listed mods was a game fix for my graphics card. Loaded it up and the game was working! After seeing trailers and other gameplay footage I was excited to see my starting planet - which was a barren rock. I quickly picked up the primary game play mechanics and started on the missions of repairing my stuff. That's where I quickly hit a roadblock. I needed 'Heridium' to repair my ship. I ventured out into a dangerous, freezing and barren planet walking towards every Waypoint in sight. I found nothing. I walked and scanned finding Carbon and Iron, Carbon and Iron, Carbon and Iron and nothing else. I looked online, thinking maybe I was missing something obvious or doing something wrong, but no - there was no Heridium to be found. So finally, after TWO HOURS of walking and scanning (occassionally hiding in a cave from the cold) I found Heridium. I mined all that I could carry, which is where I hit my next roadblock. I had to dedicate 2 more hours of walking back to my ship, while maintaining enough resources to keep my suit's life support online and having almost no inventory slots. This was a horrible and tedious process and if I hadn't already dedicated so much time to the game I would have just deleted the save and started over. So, after 4 hours I was able to repair my ship and actually start the "game." I took a break to watch some other players on YouTube and didn't find a single person who had the terrible luck I had. Most people had their ships repaired within 20 minutes or less even on their first plays. I immediately jumped to the next closest planet, knowing it couldn't be as bad as the planet I just left... and I was wrong. The next planet didn't even have enough Carbon for me to keep mining! No Carbon, no Iron and I could barely scrape together enough resources to launch my ships thrusters again so I could escape that hell. My confidence was pretty broken at that point. From, then I was playing a couple hours every night just to try and find the amazing planets and creatures I had seen in screenshots and videos. Occasionally I would break away from searching planets to follow the story line but the story seemed to take the "anything could be anything - it's so mysterious" approach and I wasn't into it. After 22 hours I finally found an interesting planet, with beaches and grass and creatures! Then I discovered I couldn't set a marker or any indicator to find that planet again. So, going back to the internet I found out that you can get the ability to set your own Waypoint IF you build a base. So could I build a base on this planet? No. So I warped around more planets until I found a place I could build a base... And of course it was on a hostile planet full of aggressive creatures and extreme heat. I did all of the grinding it requires to build it up so I could build a Waypoint, got VERY lucky and managed to find the 'good' planet again and setup a marker but by that time I was pretty burnt out on the grinding this game requires for progression. I will continue playing to finish the story but overall I couldn't recommend this game, based on the experience I've had. I give credit to Hello Games for what they have done and I think NMS is an amazing feat but I think a tighter, more focused experience would have made us all happier. It is my hope that they will develop a spin-off game with a small universe and a better focus on story telling. The game is beautiful and has some amazing moments sprinkled in, but those feel like a couple of strawberries thrown on top of the largest stale sheet-cake ever created.  Edit: The above experience was on the "Normal" difficulty setting. I did not even attempt other settings until much later.

Patch 1.3. It's good. Really! The game is much closer now to what people expected at release. Yeah, they should have labeled the game early access, and no, it's still not worth full price. Base building, vehicles, portals, space stations that are no longer weird, empty shells with a single alien staring at you. All for free, too.  It's got problems, of course... survival is till tedious. The core philosophy of the game still doesn't make sense. The game demands tribute and grinding to do ANYTHING. A million players could visit a million planets and still not see 1% of the galaxy. Yet the developers insist on putting blocks to any progress and exploration. They cannot guarantee their algorithm will make every trip interesting - that's fine! Procedural at this scale is hard - so why bother? You build a warp cell to hop to a system that is a single barren planet and you have to make another.  Want to move base? Great, you lose 50% of everything you grinded for. Unless you want to dismantle everything manually and somehow find the inventory space for it all.  Even using the new portal system requires searching nooks and crannies for glyphs.  I still recommend it. When you find an amazing planet and call it home, build a cool base, find other players, it works, even without all the nonsense of "every atom procedural". There's an interesting idea that's marred by developers worried about players seeing too much content, for no rational reason.  Buy it cheap, slap some mods on, heck use a trainer if you have to. Light up if you want. Sean Murray's insane vision is kind of here.

I made a bit of a rant review with a thumbs down after the big NEXT update, because I lost all the work I had put in to the game. I was however finally after 8 hours of frustration (searching for a tiny unmarked base station) able to restore my old save game.   If I would not have been able to play from my old save then I probably would have uninstalled the game to never play it again. It sounds like I am over reacting, but the most tedius boring grind of the game is in the first 50 hours of the game. Everything is locked away in the game and they made an excessive grind for you to complete through quests and general gameplay, before you really can start having fun in the game. I simply did not and still don't want to repeat that ever again!  So now with my old stuff intact I am trying the update out for a few days and I am having fun again. I like most new stuff in the update even though it was a lot of changes to take in. In the beginning I was not a fan of the new resources refining, but it actually makes sense and it has it's benefits.  Multiplayer feature is I hope experimental, because at this point it feels very bare bones and unfinished. You don't actually meet other players in this huge universe, but they connect to you from the starting screen. It is not an MMO setup like EVE where you always have players around you on an external server, the other player is local on your connection only. And at this point I don't think you want to run in randoms anyway due to the griefing reports that are already coming in. So I have the online mode off for now till I am at a point where I can deal with those little griefers with OP weapons and stuff.  Graphics and AI have been improved alot and also the terrain is not glitchy anymore. I used to have some occasional terrain texture glitches, but it is all smooth now. The terrain also looks a bit more diverse generated, but that might be a placebo effect :)  So yeah, I am giving the game a thumb up again. You do need to expect an excessive grind in the early game stage though and bite through that before the game starts to get fun and you have more freedom in the game. And do keep a back up of your save after the innitial grind, because stuff happens when they do a big update.

I'm going to start by saying I have my previous review of this game below, after my review of the new patch.  I enjoy space games quite a bit.  And I bought this game when it was on sale for 25 bucks.  I would recommend this game for 25 bucks, and I will explain why below.  You can also compare the review before the "Next" update and after the "Next" update.  That being said here is my review. Post "Next Patch"  After a horrible experience I really wasn't expecting much from next.  I honestly didn't think anything would be fixed.  But was pleasantly surprised by what I saw right away.  Right away I noticed that they had changed the way the game started, I only play on Perma-death mode as I like the idea of everything getting erased if you die.  It makes you play completely differently.  So the look, they completely changed the way the game looks.  It looks great.  Much better than it did.  The colors were very different.  Every planet seems to have it's own personality, and it's great.  The views of looking at the solar system from the planet is awe-inspiring.  Each creature looks great, espcially considering they are ALL randomized.  The plants as well look great, and each planet has completely different fauna and flora.  The sound is great, each monster sounds different.  The sound effects when your craft is flying around is an interesting plus.  If you're flying through a storm, you can hear the storm hitting your space plane.  The surround sound is great in the game too.  I find myself taking my headphones off because I hear something behind me, but it turns out to be the game.  The gameplay is great, they've had a long time to go over how to create controls, and I have no problems with them.  It takes a bit to get used to at first with the menu's, but you get used to it fast enough.  The tutorials on how and what to do are VERY explanative and it's great.  Alot of games get tutorials wrong, but they have done this very well, and it's built into the story mode of the game, so your story mode actually is the tutorial.  It's done well.  Now this game is a sandbox-ish game with a story mode built in.  While you CAN go and do story mode, that's not really what the game is about.  It's about going from different worlds, scanning everything in the world, and exploring the universe.  You will have the opportunity to get better gear, and craft things along the way.  The base building is new and it's a great feature.  I was expecting the building to be pre-fabricated parts that you can string together, much like subnaughtica.  But it turns out that they have that, but they ALSO have blocks that you can lay down to customize and design your own unique base.  You can make buildings out of different materials and make different type of walls and such.  All in all I would definitely recommend this game, especially when it's on sale for 25 bucks.  There are few games where you can do as much as this game for the cost.  March 14th 2018  This is a game I really wanted to like.  It was on sale for 25 bucks, so I thought I'd get it.  I have some friends who swear that they've fixed all the issues with the game and it's worth buying now.  They have multi-player, they fixed the randomization bugs, not all planets are the same.......or are they?  I like a challenge, so I started right out the gate with 1 death and you start over.  I play a little bit, die a couple times, but figure out how to get off the planet, how to use materials to make things and stay alive, how to earn a little bit of cash.  I find an abandoned ship and repair it, and it's awesome.  Much better than my old one and better than most peoples ship.  I start going through the story-line to see how that plays out and jump a couple of star systems.  I literally didn't notice, but the WHOLE time I was playing this game, my mother and brother were on teamspeak listening to me complain about things.  Finally after 20 hours of playing my mother said this verbatim "You're NOT having fun with this game, just play something else so we don't have to listen to you gripe."  Fair enough, I turned off the game, fired up Elite Dangerous, and I was happy again.  Here's my perception of what's wrong with the game.  It tries to be a base building game, but it's not.  You can't really build a base, not like you can on 7 Days to Die or Empryion, gathering minerals is extremely frustrating.  Plutonium is apparently the number 1 resource that everything uses, but to mine it, you have to aimlessly wonder about looking for it in hopes you come up to a patch and can mine it with your laser.  After spending hours of mining plutonium, I was finally able to lift off.  Then landed in another spot on my planet only to find out you need 200 plutonium to lift off the ground.  So I spend another 30 minutes mining plutonium....again....Then finally use my landing legs to bounce me into the air like a spring.....draining all the plutonium in the legs again.  Another thing No Mans sky does is it tries to be a trading game as well.  When you go to markets, you can buy or sell low or high to make a profit.  The only problem with this is, that in order to travel from system to system you have to spend hours farming for materials in order to make anti-matter, so you can turn around and mine plutonium....again....for a warp cell. Once you have one you can travel to another solar system.  If you're looking for a space trading sim than you're better look elsewhere, Elite Dangerous does probably the best job of this, and I would highly recommend it.  Now, lastly, and probably my biggest pet peeve, is the character and plant generation.  This game prided itself on being a procedural game, having everything randomized.  And when you're flying from space to the planet it's supposed to load seamlessly.  But it seems to be VERY buggy.  More times than not I would have creatures that just didn't look quite finished.  E.G.  I would have a giraffe with a short neck, a giraffe with thick legs, and a giraffe with short legs, but a long neck.  Yes there were minor differences in them all, but it was the same animal that was just spit out onto a new planet.  And when going from one planet to the next I was EXTREMELY disappointed in the fact that there was actual loading time for the planet.  They sneakily mask it in the atmospheric weather, but Empyrion does the exact same thing, just a little worse than NMS does it.  So I was able to catch what was going on.  If you want a randomized creature sim than Spore is far and away the best game every made for this, and is still fun to this day.  All in all the game tried too hard to be something that it just wasn't.  It isn't fun because it misses on so many points that you don't want to do anything in the game.  Want to trade?  Well too bad you have to mine for 2 hours to move to another solar system.  Want to mine?  Well make sure you mine for 2 hours to find your plutonium first, then you can mine somewhere.  Want to explore and find new creatures?  Well all the rocks and plants are identical with different colors.  Animals look like Dr. Frankenstein came to the world and chopped up almost every creature in the game.  Want to have fun?  Well too bad, this game isn't made for fun.  It's made to take your money.   TL/DR Version Randomizing is crap, plutonium is a word you'll hate the rest of your life, Trading isn't possible without mining.  Mining isn't possible without plutonium.  Exploring isn't possible without plutonium.  Almost every piece of anything used in the game uses plutonium.  Oh yeah, there's no plutonium "mine"  It's scattered throughout every planet so good luck finding 200 of it in one spot.  Games to consider over this game:  Elite Dangerous (for trading, exploring, and space battles) Empyrion (for base building, custom ship building, and survival experience) Spore (for creature exploration, planet terraforming, and 4x(ish) end game)

I dont even read reviews under 3 hours and my 28 hours is not enough for a good review. So I will just say this. After I learned how to handle environment issues and inventory issues....I have had those time warp moments...8-12 hours slips by because of my enjoyment. This latest update brings the game pretty close to original goals. Wanna go and explore other planets in space? this is it. Forget the survival modes, the main game is so much better. There is space combat but that is not what this game is about Explore, scan creatures and get paid, visit space stations and set up profitable trade routes.. I whole heartedly recommend.  ps. for those achievemnt type people there are plenty and they are frequent  Edit 11/1/2021  Well I play purely hardcore now. I have quite a few more hours in the game. Now I dont know why but I have not experienced a bug in 3 years. That might be because I play gmaes really slowly and have not gotten to deeper areas were bugs may live. I did loose a couple hundred hours in a save yesterday with the coolest stuff I ever owned in the game. but that was due to a power outage when I was playing because of stormy weather, not the games fault.   I really enjoy the game play. I dont consider gathering materials a "grind". In fact I personally have a problem with the overuse of that word. Zoom gamers want the end game stuff instantly. Well you got to work for it. This IS NOT grind. Grind is where you play a game and have to keep repeating exactly the same area to get enough experience to handle a more difficult area of a game. This usually only applies to mmo's that do this on purpose because they  want you to spend money so you don't have to keep repeating a portion of a map. Gathering resources and building things with those resources IS NOT grind. It's playing the game.  I swear people throw around "grind" all the time and it does not apply. It's just something with some of today's gamers where they are filled with negativity and they throw around gaming buzzwords for the sake of being negative. Obviously I have a beef with that.   Anyway I could not even begin to list all the changes and improvements this game has made since release. But there are a ton.  But for those that dont know, you basically are "different" in the galaxy and you will discover what is going on because you regain consciousness and dont remember anything. Sure that has been done a thousand times but it is a great way to tell a story by discovery.   Anyway there are 2 currencies in the game. Money (credits) and tech (nanites). Nanites allow you to improve your spacesuit, starship or your trusty multi-tool which also serves as a weapon. Credits allow you to buy better multitools and ships. But not everything can be bought so your off to mine what you can find, And remember those nanites? You scan rocks, plants and animals into an electronic catalog and earn nanites for your collected intel.   There are other ways to earn nanites but since this is a discovery game I'll let you figure it out by yourself. There are a few dangerous creatures that will attack you and pirates in space also but this is more exploration than action. Well,actually pirates will try and attack you almost any time you go into space. But they start some distance from you and you are notified and can usually flee but you CAN beat them even in the first crappy ship.   BTW that brings up another irksome review snag. I see reviewers post about how bad the ship handling is in the game. That is total ignorance. Sure your first ship flies like an out of control brick (learn to make small movements and be aware there is a delay) but compare that with an s class fighter with handling improvements which come later. you can do figure 8's around asteroid groups, turn on a dime and beat 10 to 1 odds. But no! some tried the first ship one time and summarily decided all the games space combat is terrible, sheesh. These are the same people that play a hybrid action/rpg game, have a 1 out of 10 melee skill, keep missing, because, you know 1 out of 10, and report the games hit-boxes are broken. Gamer please. Sorry for the rant  Cheers.

I came back to the game because I had heard it was updated (again) in good ways and yes, IMO it has been redeemed. There are different difficulty styles to choose from so I've noticed the game has a lot to offer to a variety of players (my 10-year-old plays this in Creative Mode, for example.)  Wow, I was mad when I wrote the old review. I'm glad I gave the game another chance.  ----------------------------  What’s the point in discovering new planets (and plants and animals), plus naming and uploading them, if there’s a good chance that the next time an update comes along they won’t exist anymore?  I remained a fan of the game even back when the pendulum was on the side of "hugely unpopular". Yes, I thought it was expensive and was disappointed in the lack of multiplayer. However, I defended it because it was a great experience.   I had the most beautiful home planet. I was so fond of the animals that inhabited it. I spent hours immersed in the place, developing an attachment to its inhabitants and "story". My entire game experience was tied to that planet because it was my base, the home I looked forward to going back to after space exploration. I had hoped that if there would ever be multiplayer, I could share it with friends.  Then the new update came along and my home is gone. The planet is technically still there with the same name but it's been replaced by an unrecognizable frozen wasteland. The plants, animals, and resources it once had have also completely changed.   It turns out that this new update has altered the game so much that our already-procedurally-generated planets have been "rerolled" to be more challenging, even if you’re playing on Normal mode like I had been. I spent hours reloading a new game, trying to generate another habitable planet like I once had, but every single one was a hellhole.   This game used to offer an amazing dreamlike experience focused on exploration and some survival. Now it’s just another survival game but with fancy filters and the promise of very limited multiplayer. With my beautiful home taken away and with every new planet trying to kill me the experience just feels depressing.  I can no longer recommend this game because I’ve lost the trust I had left in the developers. Hello Games needs to sort out what the hell their vision is and develop some better business practices.

I'm trying really hard to like No Man's Sky 1.3. Really hard. I'm doing the base building quests. I now have a dune buggy. I rehabilitated an old, crashed hauler. I'm even kinda trying to find Atlas.  But I'm not really enjoying it.  For having an infinite galaxy to explore, there is still very little to see in No Man's Sky, and that's a problem for a game about exploration. The animals and plants that I've found are all pretty samey. The environments look better than they did on the three dozen or so planets that I've explored. Every once in a while you come up on a different kind of space station or a weird new monolith to click at, but there's still very little life to the game. The planets seem to have been previously inhabited, but all of the structures appear to be isolated and expeditionary in nature. No abandoned towns or even inhabited ones.  And then there are the weird limitations. Everything is a brick wall. I wanted to explore an ancient ruin. The game put the structure at the bottom of a sinkhole on a world so cold and windy that I couldn't last 30 seconds outside the cockpit. I found a lush, verdant, temperate world full of sea to explore, but I could not find a shelter to shift my base to. I found new animal and tried to name it. The profanity filter rejected the word "bipedal."  Everything you might want to do is gated with a ridiculous time sink. Want to buy a freighter and collect different spaceships? You're going to need about 100 times the currency you are likely to have on hand. Want to jump from system to system and just explore? Prepare to grind a LOT of resources and craft a lot of fiddly stuff. Want to follow one of the game's two main quests? Fetch time!  Lots of things are deeply affected by the procedural generation of your part of the galaxy. I have tripped over no fewer than three crashed freighters and have been following their log story like is was some kind of regular feature. My friend, who has played this game since launch, has yet to see one. I recently attempted a timed quest given to me by the exocraft engineer to go find a signal 6 minutes across the map. After 5 minutes of driving across rubble and watching the camera shake like a GoPro, I fell into a hidden sinkhole and couldn't get the dune buggy back out. Rage quit.  My kid has become invested in my struggle, though. "Daddy, I hope you find enough iron or whatever."

review: No Man's Sky, A game developed and published by Hello Games, Launched 13th of August, 2016.  I have longed for a game that would allow me to take to the stars, fly amongst the raging balls of fire, the spiralling rocks and visit worlds untouched by man. I have played countless Science fiction games in hopes for this dream. And so i was obviously drawn to No Man's Sky. It's promises of grandeur and its visual style spoke to me on so many levels. But did it deliver? At first not even in the slightest, but this game has been in development for a long time now and perhaps its now finally at a point where it can be evaluated as it should be.  I would like to mention here that everything below is purely based on the game itself, I believe the team at Hello Games are doing a considerable amount of effort to make this game as good as it can be and that is a mindset that can only be praised.  [h1]Story 1/10[/h1] No Man's Sky or NMS as i'll refer to it on going isn't entirely based on a storyline, so it makes it hard to write this part. However the game doesn't really deliver any kind of information at all, as to how you came to be, where you came from or even a story of the universe you are flying through. The relatively small amount of information you are provided only seemingly leads to more questions. Not that questions aren't a good thing for a mystery and to build suspense but that's where it ends. Beyond the standard amount of information you'd expect, this game is devoid of any semblance of history, lore or world development.  [h1]Gameplay 3/10[/h1] [b]+ World Design:[/b]No Man's Sky doesn't provide a whole lot of gameplay mechanics so this section is going to be relatively short, However it does a few things particularly well and a few things pretty dismally. The world design however is pretty amazing. I understand that the worlds are procedurally generated but the algorithm used to build them is pretty sensation, the worlds are vibrant and full of things to explore. [b]+ Mining:[/b]I love a game that has a good mining system, especially when its crucial to its own mechanics. NMS has made Mining it's fundamental game mechanic in that you need to mine to do pretty much anything, from fixing your ship and ensuring you won't die, to making money. [b]+ Scanning the environment:[/b]This game has plenty to look negative toward, however i really enjoyed scanning creatures and the environment to document my travels. It felt like a great idea and never really got boring, i wish there was more of a reward for doing so than just a cash prize. But as a whole it felt very interesting, discovering different resources on a planet. [b]- Movement:[/b]NMS essentially has you moving constantly, finding resources, traversing landscapes in search of points of interest. However the mechanics here are flawed and clunky, Movement is heavy and sloppy and feels unnatural. The sprinting is almost useless as you can only really sprint for the space of 1 meter before you character collapses from the strain, and the jetpack has almost no forward propulsion only upward and even then its extremely slow and clumsy. [b]- Enemy Diversity:[/b]I use the phrase "enemy" extremely loosely here as there aren't really any enemies, the sentinel robots patrol planets occasionally and attack you if you bother them too much but there really isn't any fundamental combat set up here and the enemies aren't really worth the effort in fighting. [b]- Endgame/Purpose to Play:[/b]The game doesn't really have one, it has you progressing through this world for a seemingly endless purpose but with no reason. You can continue to build a base and upgrade your ships but there is really no purpose to it. Somewhere around the 20 hour mark you will have experienced everything this game has to offer and for a game of this scale and scope that is pretty sad. [b]- Hazardous Environments:[/b]I understand that in any survival game, the fundamental premise is that you are in a dangerous environment and that you have to survive. No one can argue with this mechanic, However in NMS you aren't really given a chance to survive, you awaken on a planet of random designation, that is in someway hostile to you. You are immediately subjected to an ever draining life system that will eventually kill you unless you can find the resources to repair your ship and to keep your exosuit functions running. I like this until you reason your character is a brick on lego wheels and that you can't traverse any sort of distance on foot without almost dying.  [h1]Visuals 5/10[/h1] NMS is a beautiful game, and it was far more beautiful at its launch. It hasn't aged extremely well although it still isn't ugly. The graphics are overtoned by its vibrant colour schemes and amount of information it throws at you almost immediately. It has a significant amount of graphical options to help alleviate even the minor discrepancies you would have, but even at Ultra this game isn't all that stunning. It looks good for what it is, but it's not breath taking, not compared to other games of this genre. There were no minor or major graphical issues in this game running it at Ultra. and the frames held steadily well above 60FPS.  [h1]Audio 7/10[/h1] Suprisingly i have very little negative to say here. NMS has provided a beautifully designed OST to compliment its game play. The world sounds alive even if you can't really see it at times which can be depressing. But the sound effects here are on point, everything you do feels impactual and connected to the world, Flying sounds intense and that first take off is stupendous to hear. Overall a sensational audio presentation here and the developers should be extremely proud of it.  [h1]Overall 4/10 "Mediocre"[/h1] Whilst No Man's Sky has had a lot of work put into it, to make it the game it should have been 5 years ago now. It's probably reached that point. However in that time games have exceeded it's original promises and have excelled at it exceptionally. It's overall mechanics and graphics are outdated and despite the the effort here to make it a great game i just can't see it becoming one. The developers are a dedicated and passionate team and the work they have put into NMS is evident from the moment you launch it. However the game isn't really worth the price, and probably not even on sale.

It's no secret that this game was panned as absolute trash when it came out. The same old cycle of gameplay from the second hour through to the last with nothing much else to do. Hello Games was rightly flamed for what they released and the blatent lies their founder made, however in the past year it's clear, even to a newer player like me, that the developers want to clear their name and give those that trusted them with their money a game worthy of that pricetag. I'm not going to say this game is perfect and it's certainly not for everyone, but it's clear it's come a long way since that disastrous launch.  Patch 1.3 adds some much-needed depth to the game, with an engaging storyline and many great tweaks and UI improvements. This was on top of a pretty fun and interesting Base-building sidestory introduced in 1.1.  As for the base game itself, don't expect an action-adventure. The game, for the most part, leaves you to your own devices when it comes to what you want to do. There's generally two main paths you can take from the start, along with the new story and the basebuilding series. On the other hand you can choose to complete missions for rep with the three races and three guilds. Or you could choose to mine some expencive metals and jump from system to system selling your wares. Or you could become a pirate, destroying other ships for their cargo.  If you played at release and were frustrated by the gameplay, now is the best time so far to come back and check it out again. If you're looking at buying this game for the first time and you're looking for a laid-back, chill, not too difficult exploration game I can recommend it at this point.  Hello games hasn't redeemed themselves for the game they initially released, but their consistant, high-quality patches and the amount of time they've spent post-release, making this game what it should've been from the start is commendable. After all, it's refreshing to see this sort of thing in an age of moneygrabbing DLC passes, yearly rehashes, lousy ports, rereleases, Pay To Win and effectively abandoned Early Access titles.

I have thought long and hard about whether I should write a review for this game or not because, frankly, I suspect the people that don't like it will never like it despite the remarkable amounts of improvement, work, and love that have gone into it since launch.  But...well, here goes.  I was one of those crazy people who bought the game on the release date for full retail price.  I am also one of those people who did not board the hype train and just took the game as it came.  I did not regret the decision to pay $60 then, and I certainly do not now.  NMS was and is as close to the game I have always dreamed of, even in its infant state from August of 2016, that has ever been developed.  Exploration.  Free will.  Mysteries.  Puzzles.  Millions of potential destinations.  Oh, and I get to be an astronaut.  I simply don't understand the hate train that is still going for this game.  I probably never will. [h1]I don't recommend No Man's Sky, even though I can't help but like it.[/h1]  I was there when it launched, I played for over 400 hours, and I definitely had some fun with it. But I just can't recommend it in 2021. The game keeps getting better and better with each new update. And Hello Games went above and beyond when it comes to fixing the game. They keep adding more features, new content, extra variety, and they're fixing bugs as well. Seemingly set on fulfilling all of their fans' fantasies. They didn't run off with the money like most AAA companies do, even despite multiple death threats and overwhelmingly negative reviews at release. And I can't praise them enough for it. I wish more developers were as passionate and hard-working as the people from Hello Games are.   No Man's Sky has a special place in my heart, I liked it even when it came out all broken and downgraded. It always gave me a sense of tranquility and inner peace. Just walking around and listening to the music, looking for the next interesting thing in the distance. Taking screenshots and slowly building up my base - it's a pretty unique feeling. And there's a decent amount of things that you can do. Here are some of my favorites:  🟢 finish all the main storylines 🟢 unlock all inventory slots and fully upgrade your suit 🟢 find the best ship and multi-tool and then upgrade them as well 🟢 build a big base and learn all the blueprints 🟢 max out your relationships with all the alien races 🟢 get the best freighter and all the frigates 🟢 become an intergalactic billionaire 🟢 visit at least one of each planet type 🟢 ride some animals and cook some foods 🟢 complete Nexus missions and unlock all the quicksilver items 🟢 customize your character's appearance 🟢 grow your own living ship and fly around in it 🟢 scavenge an abandoned freighter 🟢 construct and upgrade all the terrain vehicles 🟢 manage a flourishing settlement 🟢 get a maximum wanted level on foot and in space 🟢 explore the deepest oceans and find the weirdest looking anomalies 🟢 take advantage of the photo mode 🟢 unlock everything and collect at least one of each item in the game  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2626396217   But no game is perfect. And, unfortunately there are massive downsides to consider as well. Many of which are too big for me to ignore:  🔻 terrible story, very boring, a lifeless cliche 🔻 no memorable characters or lines of dialogue 🔻 everything is text based, extremely dull and uninspired 🔻 instead of seeing a character punch you, your screen flashes red and you read about being punched, that sort of thing 🔻 there is no voice acting or cutscenes or even first-person hands/body 🔻 you're just a floating gun with no personality because your choices have no meaning 🔻 very buggy and often requires googling solutions 🔻 extremely dated visuals, even on the highest settings and using enhancement mods 🔻 most choices are either "proceed" or "postpone and do it later anyway" 🔻 boring achievements and in-game challenges 🔻 repetitive gameplay loops, doing the same thing over and over again 🔻 awful animations, lots of clipping and lacking in impact (this is one of the worst offenders in my opinion) 🔻 Unreal Engine 3 makes everything look like plastic 🔻 bad draw distance, things constantly popping up right under your feet 🔻 multiplayer is terrible, everyone is cheating, and I recommend instantly disabling it 🔻 there's no online anti-cheat or security, people can just force resources into your backpack or use mods that change the rules of the game 🔻 timed expeditions that offer exclusive rewards, and then locking that content out (FOMO for some people)  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2626396179  I understand that at it's core, No Man's Sky is still a single-player game. And it's every player's choice on whether to cheat or mod their game. I used some visual enhancements myself, and I'm glad Hello Games is cool with people modding their game. Moreover, if you're OK with all the downsides I listed, and you still want to play it - go for it! It's not a bad game, I'm just very conflicted about it.   Even though I still like No Man's Sky, I secretly wish that they would just stop updating it. Make No Man's Sky 2 instead, with an engine from this decade. And a proper story with a bigger emphasis on player choice and emotional impact. Invest some of that money into better animations and bug fixes. You've done the impossible once, maybe you can do it again. With a team as determined and creative as Hello Games, I'm sure you can pull it off. But for now, this is where I say goodbye to No Man's Sky.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2628855466

I was very eager to play No Man’s Sky when it came out in August 2016 -- not because of the hype, but because of the ability to fly around in space, land on a planet, explore and discover alien creatures, only to return to space and visit another planet intrigued the nerdy kid side of me! I put down the game around Halloween 2016 to kill zombies and play other games relevant to the season. I forgot about NMS until I picked it up in June. I was really enjoying getting back into the game, building a base, and working through the Specialist missions. I had exocraft pads on several planets, was about to start farming, and had plans to save up for a freighter -- and was ready to give the game a glowing, thumbs up review.  That was all before the Atlas Rising Update; this game is no longer simple, chill, or enjoyable!! While the Update has added a few cool new features (like side jobs and improvements to the in-flight radar), much more has been introduced or modified that makes the game a complex mess!. The arbitrary changes to resource names, unnecessary modifications to the Analysis Visor and the interaction interface, the Mr. Fix-It interface to open Cargo Crates & Damaged Machinery [that pulls me out of the game a little], the unwelcome changes to the Discoveries menu, the addition of factions/guilds and system economies, the general wonkiness of flying a ship, and the loss of all the Specialists in my base - and resetting my progress with them - makes me very upset & annoyed! Game updates shouldn’t change things this much… especially for a game not in Early Access!!! (And I thought switching to Iron to recharge the Pulse Drive was going to be the worst change introduced by an update!?)  Actually, with the latest update NMS is giving me EVE Online vibes. EVE was a boring, complex mess that I quit playing after a few months. But, to be fair, EVE updates didn’t change things so drastically.  I’ll move on to other games on my To-Play list. If I do ever come back to NMS, it will be a long way down the road and only after I get the taste of alienation out of my mouth!  EDIT: 10/31/2019 I reinstalled the game to give it another shot. After a couple hours I just couldn't get into it. The game may look & feel better... but it still doesn't excite / intrigue me like the original

Review update:  It's been over 5 year since my review. At the time of writing they had done their 3rd mayor free update. A few days ago they released their 21st (!) major update for FREE. There is no sign of stopping. These developers are RELENTLESS in their persuit to update the game. It's not longer just exploring and base building (which both also have improved). You can manage a town, manage your massive fleet or big ships, be a pirate, scavenge abandoned freighter ships, play a roguelite mode and much much more. The graphics have been updated several times, better graphics options added, planets have been made to be more diverse including the wildlife.  Most other games would have asked money for this content in the form of many years of season passes. These updates are FREE. Every.....single....one! There must be a catch right? For there are cosmetics in the game. Surely you'd have to buy premium currency for that? NO...SORRY that currency for extra cosmetics can only be earned by daily and weekly missions in the form of quick silver.  You buy the game once...everything is included for free. Making it one of the best deals in the industry. Hello Games....thank you for making me feel valued as a player and paying customer. You've become a absolute prime example of how the games industry should treat the player.  Original review below. ------------------------------- These guys made lot's of promisses for a hyped game and when the game came out they did not deliver. For a long time it's been "No Man's Buy" for me. They could have easily take the money and ran and lived their days in infamy. Did did not do this however, it seems they are serious about this game and believe in it.   Now with this latest frankly huge update the game looks what it needs to be. Worth $60 now? Not really, but the recent updates are a definite step in the right direction. However, no matter how many updates come out, this is definitely not a game for everyone.   PROS: -A practically infinite, procedurally generated universe to explore -An advertised 30-hour storyline -Side missions to keep you occupied while exploring -Base building that is woven into the story -Limited multiplayer allowing you to run into other players, as well as come across their bases and discoveries -Relaxing music and atmosphere -Multiple difficulty levels that caters to more hardcore and casual playstyles -Regular patches and updates -Mod support  CONS:  -Gameplay can be grindy and repetitive  -Every system has a space statiion, ruining the sense of isolation -When flying, the game will try to adjust where to fly for you to prevent you from crashing. This doesn't always work out, and usually just prevents you from going where you want and you end up crashing anyway. -Procedural generation can yield pretty odd results -Mission objectives tend to just be fetch quests -Inventory management can be a chore, especially during the early game -Despite regular patches, the game still has its fair share of bugs   Despite a horrible launch, Hello Games has shown that they care about the future of No Man's Sky. I believe that even on launch day, there was a good game deep inside here, it just needed refinement to show. As of 1.3, No Man's Sky is beginning to find its identity, and is starting to deliver the potential it showed on launch. I picked up the game on sale last week, and have enjoyed a good majority of the 50 hours I've clocked in on it. For this reason, I feel it's safe for me to recommend this.   HOWEVER, I do NOT believe this game is worth $60 yet. There is still more that needs to be expanded upon before I can safely say that. If the price drops to around 30 or 40 bucks, then I say go for it. There's plenty of content here to make you feel like you've got your money's worth, but it's still not anything groundbreaking, and still has its fair share of problems.   As I've said, this is a game that definitely isn't for everyone. Combat takes a back seat to the exploration and resource gathering here. This is advertised as a chill exploration experience for good reason; it's more Star Trek than it is Star Wars. If you enjoy walking sims, survival games, exploration in Elite: Dangerous, and games similar to Minecraft, there's a chance you'll dig this game.

Great game! I know this game started out with a lot of unfulfilled hype, but in the time since its launch, the features that were desired have been added (with the final features to be added with the NEXT update on July 24th).   Having played the game for over 500 hours in a month ands a half, I have experienced almost no bugs or problems. I have greatly enjoyed my journey in NMS. The story is good - not mind-blowing, but decent. The gameplay is relaxing most of the time, but with plenty to do, quests to complete, and places to explore. If you are the type of player who can set goals for yourself, enjoy gathering, survival, building, exploring, and so forth - this is the game for you!   On the other hand, if you need to have someone hold your hand, constant story, or punishing PvP - don't bother. That's not to say that PvP isn't in the NEXT update - it is! But it isn't designed to be punishing. NMS is primarily designed to be a cooperative game. Sure, you can kill othewr players, but the rewards aren't going to be that great, and the punishment to the other player aren't going to be that significant. This won't be a game where you can "camp newbs" and enjoy griefing others. If you need that, go play Eve: Online. Great game specifically designed for that sort of play. Which is why I hated it. I am not a big fan of PvP. I don't enjoy griefing, or being griefed. That's just not my style of play, and I don't enjoy it. But some people do - and that's fine for them. I'm glad that there are games out there that they can enjoy. But this isn't one of them.  So if you enjoy exploration, building, gathering, survival, challenging and setting goals for yourself (there's even a permadeath mode, if you want to really punish your mistakes) - this is a great game! If you want to reward a developer that didn't have to stick around and work hard to make up for their mistakes - this is a good opportunity to do so! Hello Games could have taken the money and closed down when they started to get death threats over the things that weren't in the game. But they didn't. They stuck around and worked on getting those things in. Now, I'm not saying that they shouldn't have done a better job back in 2016. I'm saying that they didn't take the easy way out. They stuck to it and put in what was missing. Not every game company does that. Just look at all the abandoned Early Access games on Steam.   Personally, I'm enjoying NMS. I will likely be starting a brand new playthrough come the new update in a couple days. I think that it will be a fantastic experience!  Note: I've seen some reviews complaining about how they can't seem to get the game to run well on their computers. I find that odd, considering that I got my computer back in 2012, and it runs just fine. Sure, I've upgraded the video card to a GTX 1080, but if people with fancy, flashy, gaming computers are having problems... either there are driver issues, or something is going on. I have yet to have any performance issues.

Day one player here.  I liked the game at release, and it keeps getting better.  Get it on sale, and don't look back.  The devs have added so much, and are not finished.    The most amazing part about this game is the concept of the 18 trillion planets, and the procedural generation.  The cynical may say that 2 hours in, and you've seen everything.  I will admit that I leave a lot of planets within ten minutes, but I may be losing out.  I have hundreds of hours now, and still find novel things, and lots of awesome sights.  Then you think, once I leave, it's likely that no one will ever see this planet again.  It's kind of profound and humbly for a video game.  If this sounds cool to you, it's worth the $60.  It's definitely worth $25.  Compared to discovering a unique universe, what's a couple of bucks?

You might be surprised at some of the things I don't regret doing. One of them was buying this game at launch at full price. Whether it had to be released by a deadline according to a contract, or because the development team ran out of money and had to release [i]something[/i] to keep from starving, the game as it was caused . . . several . . . people to raise the perfectly valid complaint that the game felt unfinished. Some even leveled the accusation, now all but proven false, that the development team were greedy liars. If the developers had enough time to make and release the game as it exists today, no one would have complained. If today's No Man's Sky was the first release of No Man's Sky, the mountain of negative reviews on this page would not exist. If this was the first version of the game the world at large knew, it would have been praised by perhaps not all, but a substantial portion of the haters. Now, obviously, that's not what happened, and the existence of previous versions is now a canon part of the lore, but you shouldn't judge a game by what it was, you should judge it by what it is. No Man's Sky is beautiful. No Man's Sky is thrilling. No Man's Sky is compelling. No Man's Sky is just a little scary now and then. No Man's Sky is complete. But that's not to say No Man's Sky is over, not by a long shot. No Man's Sky is back, and it's here to stay.

Preface:  I pre-ordered No Man's Sky and I won't get into the philosophical debate as to who said what/when/how/why many people balked at the game after its release. I pre-ordered the game expecting exactly what I paid for at release. A walking sim in a procedurally generated universe with some space travel and stuff to explore. I DID NOT expect it to have multiplayer...or craftable bases...or vehicles outside of shipe for interstellar travel...or even a marketplace of any kind. What I knew was that I was going to be dropped off in some backwoods, probably uncharted, neck of a galaxy with nothing. No instruction manual, no guides...truly alone and free to explore MY game. Statistically I shouldn't have been able to find anyone, so I could play the game as it was sold to me. Alone in the universe. There is no winning the game. It isn't even the point of the game. It was made to explore. Statistically, the population of the game at launch was zero and remains zero. I'll come back to that statement in my review which is as follows...   Cons: No "instruction manual" is provided with the game. You are completely in the dark with regard to everything, which includes base building/weapon upgrades/ship upgrades/inventory management/mostly commonly needed materials to keep you alive. Base building is not as intuitive as it could be, so practice what you want in creative mode. Inventory management, though greatly improved, is still a monster to deal with in early game as you have to purchase inventory expansion slots (which have been immensely expanded since launch), which requires you to scan everything and upload it as well as mine a great deal of materials to sell in order to purchase the expansions. The oceans look like garbage compared to release. Hello Games needs to fix the garbage that is the surface of oceans. Ship handling can be a bit of a trial as different ships handle differently to noticable effect. There is "was" a huge learning curve with regrd to all these things, but many QoL patches/Wiki's/Forums since launch have made it much less daunting. Everything is useful in the game, which often leads to overstuffed pockets causing a inventory management crisis. If you run a mod that substantially changes planetary formation and star density, do not expect anything to be where it was, or the same size and type it was before mod removal. Yes, I have lost planets and have also saved game on the surface only to log in within a planets core with the only hope of escape being reloading a previous save. The games price point is too high, especially for a game that is almost 2 years out. Players really should have customizable avatars but do not. Lastly, THE HATE IS REAL! If you purhase this game and enjoy it, a multitude of people unsatisfied with it at launch, will harass every forum (almost daily) stating why you shouldn't like it and the specific reasons why you are an idiot/sheeple/got conned.   Pros:  The player community is real. The people who have stuck with this game have built upon it and improved the experience for everyone involved through creation of mods and easily accessible guides to ease new players into the game. There is no instruction manual to this game and that is a Pro. The graphics are crisp and stylized, The creatures DO NOT walk on their heads or other ridiculousness that I have seen evidence of of. I never had an issue with the game graphically or with the procedural generation of the entire game. Stalking creatures stalk, docile creatures will attempt to kill you if you attack their young, some creatures travel in family units while others are loners. The game supports Mods and there are quite a few really nice ones. There is a terrific story to the game that you literally have to find and put together yourself. You can build bases on freighters and own up to 6 ships which can dock on your freighter. There is quite a bit of variation with regard to ships and the weapon you carry. There are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS. All updates have been free. You can call your ship to you from anywhere on the planet, including the freighters. Inventory management is much better. And lastly, there isn't (FIXED since to original review) multiplayer. There are those who swear off this game because it didn't have it and realistically, at the time of launce, no one should have thought it was going to be there. The population of the game remains a zero sum. A percentage of this game that is so close 0% that it could be read a zero. Why would anyone think a game with zero players in an almost infinitely large space would have multiplayer functionality? which is another Pro to some: they added multiplayer functionality to the game. The game is as easy or hard as you'd like to make it. The story is written in fragments written by 5 different "civilizations" and it is incentive to looking for them.  It is a walking sim with space exploration that allows YOU to make all the decisions. Don't care about story then that is fine. Don't look for one. Want to kill every living thing on a planet, you can do that also. If you DO want to find these things...its all there if you want it to be. I really enjoy this game and recommend it to everyone.

Glad I waited for $23 and 1.3 patch.  There's a Bizzaro-World image of NMS.  It's called ELITE: DANGEROUS.  It, too, has this massive, procedurally-generated galaxy.  It, too, uses procedural rules to generate much of its content.  And it, too, is a mile-wide-and-inches-deep design; e.g. a very repetitive core gameplay loop.  But, unlike NMS, its main focus is one ship combat/upgrades and trading.  Exploration is given short shrift in ED, and building is nonexistent.  Resourcing gathering is a sad, grindy pastime required for PvP competitiveness.  Yes, PVP.  NMS swaps that around.  Ship combat/upgrades are as light as a feather.  Only a fool would try to establish a "profitable" trading loop in NMS, thanks to the difficulty of warping between systems.  NMS is all about exploration, resource gathering, and base building.  And, unlike ED, there's a barebones tutorial/story to take the place of any PVP activity.  Like I said, mirror images of each other.  One all po-faced and military and stuff, one all full of bloom and shiny things and goofy alients.  If someone would, someday, mash the two games together, that would truly be a reason (along with being able to perform oral sex on oneself) to never leave the house.

I purchased the game after a couple updates for a sale price around $35. At that point, the game felt worth that price.  With the 1.3 update, No Man's Sky finally feels like what I want it to be. There are still some small places I would change, but the game is a lot of fun. The questing system gives new purpose to a game that was previously all about exploration. For the current $24 price, I would definitely pick it up. For the full $60 price, I would hesitate unless the exploration aspect really speaks to you.  Make no mistake, Hello Games hasn't given up on the game and it isn't the same title that we saw at launch.  edit: And with 1.5, the game is basically brand new. Like I said, HG hasn't given up on the game.

You'll get almost all of the value out of the game in the first few hours. After that, it's boring repetition. This isn't like Minecraft in Space. You mine for things, but you can only repair things or build things if you have blueprints for it. They added a few new things with some free content patches, which essentially put into the game things that were supposed to be there in the first place, but there are still advertised features missing.  It doesn't run all that well, and there's really nothing to do. The aliens you meet are meaningless. The technology you get blueprints for is meaningless. There is no significance to anything other than get stuff so you can get more stuff so you can leave it behind when you leave to get more stuff in the next place, as you go toward the center, where then you'll just repeat the cycle, over and over.  I cannot, in good concious, recommend this at full price, or even half price. The new content does not add enough to justify the price. The combat is poor and the enemies are dull. The proceedural generation means large amounts of nothing, between animals and plants that all look the same, to rock formations that look the same, to caves full of random crystals you don't need. Nothing in this game is anything but lonely boredom. And maybe that's it's message, but that's not fun, and that makes it a terrible game.  Not only at this price, but at the cost of your wasted time.

NOTE: I bought this game at the onset of Atlas Rises Update, and am now updating this review as of 9/23/21.  I was told about this game from a friend of mine who also plays open world survival games. I have a deep love for the genre and its provided me countless hours of enjoyment in virtual worlds. When the release date actually arrived, I found myself caught in a dilemna because it became readily apparent just how much of a stir Hello Games prompted but didn't deliver. I felt that the community reacted very poorly to it. I didn't purchase it back then.  If there is one thing that life has taught me in all my years is that is okay to let things cook for a little while longer in the event you find them mostly incomplete. In the age of Pre-alpha and beta games (I refuse to buy into them) I've really noticed a hot trend of garbage games coming into their own over time. That is usually when I'll buy into them. This also allows me to skip and fast forward past the Content Zergs who overload servers and then leave and go whine on the forums why things didn't work out for them. I just can't be a part of that anymore. Coincidentally I also never see movies on opening night either.  I'm so glad I waited. While I do notice that large groups of vocal folk will pass this game over because of its procedural generation (a common complaint is how random but formulaic procedural generation is, and they'd be correct to say so.) the real reward in my humble opinion is on the strange and rare occasions where things just fall into place. That's the real gold and often the food for some of the most wonderful screenshots that players conjure. Sure you'll run into a droning system of odd analogues but then there's always that one memorable system that totally jumps at you. Those are fun feels for creative people, and I consider that my meat and drink in No Man's Sky.  The Good is that many difficulties and goals are now overcome, and the developers (Sean Murray included) continue to press on and make their game better. In a year if I look back, I wonder how far have the changes gone? Will I even recognize old haunts anymore? There are already reviews in play that already say so from a year back from players that bought in at launch. Multiplayer has been finally realized, and while shaky at first, it's become a pretty solid addition to the game.  Also, the fact that ships are also highly customizable and can be built from the floor up (although not from scratch im afraid.. missed opportunity here!) from their basic model shows that this aspect has come a very long way.  There is a fair amount of tradeskilling, from basic components to whole base structures and this was some fantastic icing on an otherwise very bland system that it had in Atlas Rises.  The Bad is that there are still some bugs that really impact the little things. Collision and hit box sizes can be janky but mostly not harmful unless you find yourself slipping through the terrain (or your ship) into the netherworld. Procedural generation has had several upticks in what it can do, but somehow I can come across creatures from multiple different planets and star systems, yet are still eerily familiar.  I'm looking at you, flying sky crabs!   While I enjoy the idea of being able to now tame and ride pets, I find them somewhat not terribly useful.  It's actually quite more rewarding to tame things you might never use except for cute value.  Also, customizing your pets doesn't seem to really add much outside of aesthetics.  Hello Games should likely look into this in future updates so they can actually mean something.   The currency system is decent, and I find myself easily able to restart old saves without having to worry about older currencies becoming obselete.  No matter how much cash you think you have, it will go.. and fast!  The Ugly is when the new and the old community clash. That's really the only thing that goes beyond reason for me. Listening to the complaints of the first buyers and the overly whiny negativity gets old really fast. Many of those folks just haven't gotten over their own disappointment. Troll Culture is en vogue and critique with thoughtlessness brings everything down; even things you might normally enjoy. Negativity is viral. Wait for a sale if you are skeptical.
