At the time of my initial review, was clocking in at 340 hours with this game, and I've completed all the main and side quests. I'm not filthy rich, but im comfortable enough to spend most of my time tweaking my basebuilding skills, or just exploring. I'm an avid shiphunter. The theme and the story are very much couched in existentialism. You're an explorer in a vast universe. Why are you there? What are you doing? If those are not questions you are willing to wrestle with in No Man's Sky, then the game might not be for you.  At the time of my current review, I have clocked in over double the old time and I am filthy rich now, but somehow the questing has taken a back road.  I've missed some things in some of my playthroughs, and I find old quests tend to get reset pretty often if you delete old bases and backtrack locations yield new positions for those quests.  This sometimes confuses me, but I feel this is likely the result of having to find ways to reconcile old and new content.  I doubt it is going to roadblock brand new players when they first join the game.  But to re-iterate, the vastness is compelling when it does come together. Warping over to the next galaxy hoping to see and interact with something unique? Suddenly, a violent storm or attack sends you on a spiral? The best times in the game for me are when I'm struggling. If that has any appeal to you, then No Man's Sky is definitely for you.

It's not a bad game, it is just not a good game. I am glad I got it on sale, it is NOT worth the $60 retail price, it is not an AAA game by any stretch of the word. If you can get it for 50% off or more, it is worth the price.   It breaks no new ground, it is not really a building game, it is not really an exploration game, it is not really a survival game, it is not really a space/economy game, it is not really a space fighting simulator. Yet it is all these, but because none of these things are done well, it falls very flat.  It is illogical in play; the NPC are lifeless and random. The planets all looks the same after a few are explored. The building is limited. The mining is repetitive. The economy trading is not based on any logical system I could determine. The story is lackluster and trite. The ideas are all recycled. The graphics are generic and repeated over and over.  But at the same time, it doesn't really fail at any of these things either. Although I am lead to understand I am playing it after much more additional work has been done, and it was much worse at launch.  I dislike only having an up or down vote for it, as it is 'meh' great way to waste some time.

[Update Dec 2018, NEXT and stuff...]  Update has excellent multiplayer features, dogfighting, combat, missions, quests, basebuilding, crafting, exploring, grinding, mining, and is a lot of fun.  My only complaint is lack of joystick support for the excellent space combat, and progress seems to really hit a wall and slow down a lot at a certain point, when there's still so much cool stuff you could build or buy that seems out of reach. Certain critical resources are very hard to find, and in other cases, prices are very expensive compared to how much you're bringing in. Maybe it's just a matter of "git gud."  I liked this game before. It's improved a lot since then, I still heartily give it a thumbs up. 4/5. If progression was a little more straightforward and/or smoother, and it had joystick support, it would be a 5.  [Previous Review Below...]  I was one of the ones who stayed on the sidelines while this game was being developed, then when it was released to mixed or negative reviews. I don't know how bad it was before, but I can say it's quite a bit of fun now. There's a steady sense of progression from the very first moment. As you make your way around your starting planet, then to other planets, then to other systems and space stations, the game places objectives before you to help lead you towards more and more self-reliance. Maybe this game gets bad after x number of hours, but after 4.5 hours it's still nice and intriguing. There's a mystery to solve, ancient structures to explore, and as you do so you continue to unlock more technology to help along the way.  Technically the game is fine. I'm running on Win7 x64 with an i7-6700k, 32MB RAM, and GTX 980 video card. I get a solid 60FPS everywhere, but I'm never super aggressive on graphics settings. Give me high res textures with anisotropic filtering and I'm happy. This game has pretty extensive quality settings, so you're sure to be able to tune it to your system with no problems.  I only have two minor complaints so far about the gameplay. First, the inventory is very limited, and the stack sizes are relatively small compared to how much material you'll need for your journey. For this reason you end up spending quite a bit of time gathering resources and juggling inventory. This was one of the initial complaints and it's still a bit annoying. There are ways to upgrade your personal inventory capacity, and you will eventually find bigger ships. You can transfer inventory directly to your ship from anywhere. After about 3-4 hours I did find a ship that was able to hold twice as much cargo, but almost all the slots are locked and require quite a few credits to unlock.  My other complaint, and this is purely a matter of personal preference, is that the universe is rather lonely. There are NPCs to interact with, but so far I haven't been forming any relationships, and they're all very alien in appearance. I like games with NPC companions, like Mass Effect and the like, but this game just has you against a mostly hostile or indifferent universe. There is an NPC that shows up for regular appearances as a matter of story, but I wouldn't call him/her a companion by any means. Being able to form a crew and having RPG options wouldn't go amiss in my book, but that can hardly be a mark against this title.  Travel times are pretty acceptable, with four different speed options - cruising, which requires you to constantly hold your thrust button down, a boost speed which is kind of like afterburners, but it lasts as long as you have fuel, a phase drive which is kind of a sublight speed, and then warp drive, which almost instantly takes you from one star system to the next. Going from space to atmosphere, then down to the surface and back is a smooth process with no hitching or jarring transitions. If your angle is too steep, you'll get a burning aurora effect around the edges of your viewable area, along with some shaking and creaking sounds, which is a cool touch. So far it appears to be visual only.  You also get a scanner, which can be upgraded. At first it will detect materials and points of interest within a certain radius. If you aim at a planet you can scan it and see what conditions to expect, and what kinds of materials are most abundant there. All planets I've found so far have the essentials - iron, carbon, and plutonium, which you need in order to maintain your various energy levels and conduct basic repairs. It's the more exotic materials you'll see as the result of a long distance scan.  In my time of playing I have never found a planet that wasn't hostile enough to drain your environmental systems while you're on foot. This system is like a hunger or thirst meter that runs down constantly. Sometimes there will be storms or something that makes it go down even faster. This means you can't venture out too far from your ship or the nearest shelter without either going back to let your bar fill back up again, or using some of the materials you've picked up to refill it out in the field. I'm sure there are M class planets around somewhere but I've yet to discover any.  Overall this is a pretty decent game. It's good enough that I can see putting 20-40+ hours into it at least. We'll just have to see beyond that. I haven't tried the new multiplayer features, but if that system is developed enough it might be a blast to do some base building with friends or family. We'll see. So far though, it's a pretty solid game, easily worth picking up on sale at least. The current sale price of $24 seems like a pretty good bargain for something like this, but I don't know if I'd go much higher than that.

Rewriting my review for the NEXT update. I last played this a year ago and thought it was pretty neat even back then, took a long break since and when I came back it had drastically changed from the core. The game's been massively improved since launch and it's no overstatement that they have released updates as big as full expansions to the game for free. Gotta respect the devs a lot for that instead of giving up.  Since NEXT I found planet generation and gameplay to have become a lot more interesting. Nothing I've found has really been the same and I've found massively varied worlds, even with those of same type there's a good chance terrain, fauna etc. generation makes it very distinct from each other - I can't hold off taking screenshots like a junkie :P. The game really nails that feel of awe and discovery I haven't really felt in other games much before. No other gameplay experience I've had really compares to this, I'm just enjoying going from planet to planet and seeing what crazy things they have to offer (while planning on what to do next). I'm playing on Survival mode too so there is some challenge involved gathering resources, especially on extreme worlds, and the game now has an overarching 'story' with objectives that teach you most of the basic systems as you go on and give you an incentive to explore more of the galaxy.  I feel like they added a lot more purpose to the game now. Since you can create bases on any planet you want with almost unlimited building you always have something to work towards, and if base building isn't your thing then you can go and upgrade your ship or raid freighters, or just explore and continue the story. It's still a very chill exploration game, only the start of the game can be harsh outside creative mode, but I didn't really mind it, it's necessary to get used to the game's systems. There's also a lot more NPCs and quests added, even base building itself is a long series of quests, and it's neat that you can continue it across multiple planets so if you decide you want to move, you can have your crew teleport to another location.  There is functional multiplayer co-op too so I'd say it has something for everyone as long as you don't mind the gathering/crafting, that still hasn't changed from the launch but has gotten quality of life updates. I'm very interested in seeing where the game will go in the future since it would even make a pretty good MMO if they expanded their systems, they kind of have a base for that already since you can upload your discoveries and bases and you can travel to other people's stuffs. I very much like it as a singleplayer game too though.  EDIT: Another thing they should definitely add is workshop support for modding, the potential for mods for this would be insane.

At launch, this game really was not worth it even at 80% discount - now, at 50% discount this was a pleasant buy, the story is engaging, the controls despite their console feel work well, and overal the game is very smooth.  Of course, this game is still far from perfect, there is very little variation from one world to the next, missions start to feel repetitive really fast, and the whole exocraft mechanic feels tacked on, introducing 2 unique crafting ingredients that even within exocrafts are barely used at all, and despite the effort required to unlock these ingredients they are almost without value in the market place.  The money system is perhaps my next complaint, the way it is currently setup means you spend 90% of the early game grinding for 10 minutes to fill your inventory, spend another 10 minutes going to a space station and selling your loot, then repeating this a dozen times until you finally have the millions of credits needed to perform a single ship or multitool upgrade that is actually worth making. The economy needs major work, as most non-grindy credit sources are from exploration, giving at best some 5000 credits, a mere drop in the bucket of your average 1.5 million credits needed to upgrade your ship to next the level - not even considering the hundreds of millions needed to get yourself a freighter.  Another complaint is the base system, what is there is incredibly well designed, but there is honestly very little to actually do. Once more a situation that feels like exocraft happens, in that a whole bunch of ingredients are needed for the base building process, but those ingredients are not balanced into the rest of the game properly, causing a heavy dissonance that breaks immersion.   All in all, if you enjoy space, exploration and a compelling story supported by a good PC-friendly control scheme, then go and buy this game at 50% off, but I cannot recommend this game, even now, at the full price tag, not until helloGames gets around to really integrating all the separate parts of this game into a proper whole.  Edit 13 April 2020: Great progress has been made on most of my down points, unfortunately with the Abyss update they once  more repeated the process of adding new items which are only used for a specific situation, hopefully they will better integrate these items as they have previously done for the other resources added by such updates.  My main remaining issue is how repetitive the procgen starts to feel after only a few solar systems, I feel the game would benefit greatly from some dedicated improvements in this area.  As of this time, I'd say the game is worth it at 30% off, but they have yet to reach the point where I'd be willing to pay full price for it.  Edit 4 December 2024: I still have my issues with Abyss and the lack of integration on those resources, but so much new content has been added, good content, that on the whole I truly do believe this game is worth it without discount by this point.  That is not to say it is a game for everyone, but if you want what is decisively the *best* space exploration game, where you can visit every inch of it's insane amount of planets and galaxies (Even if those inches wont be 100% unique), build to your liking, and do it all alone or together, then this is the game for you.

It`s too bad I spent the full $60 at release and had to wait many months for any considerable work to be done, but better late than never I guess. I think once full blown multiplayer and co-op is established, and the animals (oh, those animals) get an AI overhaul the game will certainly be worth the $60+.    In conclusion, while the game has made an amazing recovery from the initial backlash it got on release, there are still some patches needed to really flesh it out as the game Hello Games wanted, but I am quite optimistic at this point which is great because it was hard to find optimism for this game several months ago.  Yes I recommend, but if you`re uncertain I`d say wait for a few more patches if you really want bang for your buck.

Each planet has the same half a dozen types of things to find, and you quickly max out your ship, suit and weapon and then it becomes pointless. From what I understand some of the upgrades like Atlas and Pathfinder improved it...can't imagine what it was like before them.  If they would keep adding planet/flora/fauna/ship/weapon/etc. types and add cities and civilizations (even abandoned ones) it would keep me going on it, but at the moment, I'm done.  If that kind of time is all you want, its fine, but being billed as a limitless game with a quintillion different planets is kind of a half truth.

I was a pre-order buyer. I fell for the hype and was burned. Hello Games will never deliver on the original game promise, despite what paid for game magazine articles tell you.   To their credit Hello Games has stuck with this and tried to make it better. They have done a lot, but now we're getting to the point where their enthusiasm doesn't make up for their lack of competency.  They're good natured people but mostly incapable of fixing their base game and I honestly would never buy another of their products ever again.   7 years of updates and basic issues have persisted since launch.  They've added many updates, most are content islands that don't interact well with the rest of the game. Some invalidate previous game systems, and almost every one of the updates has disrespected player investment forcing changes to previous saves and accomplishments. I've had to re-do major questlines in a save because they decided they wanted to make the grind more tedious.   Quest hooks still fail to work correctly 1 in 3 times, 7 years later. Any session is moments away from a glitch that will force you to exit and reload in hopes of the game actually working right. That's just basic functionality. Still falling through floors because they can't get collision checking working correctly, 7 years later.   They've somehow managed to court and appeal to a community that thinks reloading save games for 4 hours to try and finally get a rare random spawn is entertaining.   So much of the game is tedious work- it has all the hallmarks of annoying inconvenient mobile pay2win app gaming design without any of the pay-to-skip / pay-for-convenience functionality available. It's truly baffling to me.   They did finally add in some difficulty and customization options to remove some parts of the game but the resulting product isn't worth booting up. It's so shallow and empty of reward.   And the Artemis main quest story is the one of the worst, I'm 14 and this is deep, writing experiences I've ever encountered. The fact that it's mandatory to unlock most of the game is inexcusable. It is straight out of a 2000s LiveJournal blog.   Most things are save-game specific and updates have had a tendency to ruin previous saves, so you can see where that timed play number comes from.  I've given them the benefit of the doubt but it is such a shallow vapid experience and worst of all- it has no concept of what fun is.

The fact that Hello Games did not take the money and run, but took the money and fueled it back into this game and delivered each update at no cost to the gamers is, in my book, VERY commendable. The launch may have been poor, but they have learned from it and have become a better company for it.   If you are on the fence on whether or not to buy this game due to the fiasco at launch. The game is NOT like it was. It is far better. Now that VR will be a feature soon as well as true multiplayer, This is, for sure, the game to get.   BUY IT! You will be glad you did.

I bought this game for €24 on sale and I don't consider it worth the price. What I did for the first 3 hours: - Wait in a 5 minute "loading shaders" screen - Spent the next 3 hours collecting resources in extremely repetitive manner - Get a hyperdrive - Dealt with sub-par ship controls - Feel incredibly isolated due to no voice acting at all  By the time I hit my second solar system I just ALT+F4'd it.  There are much better open-world survivor games out there right now. It might be worth €15 or under. Not terrible, but not woth €24, definitely not worth €50.

I have been playing No Man's Sky since it's release day on PS4. I eventually switched to PC after the first or second major update and haven't regretted it.  Honestly, if you don't mind a relaxing, do almost whatever you want kind of space exploring game, then why the hell are you even here?  This game is just a nice space exploration game with some story elements thrown in to keep you going. However, that doesn't mean it's bad. Oh no, on the contrary in fact...  This game is everything I could ask for in a space game. -Ships -Goals -Randomized planets -Randomized animals -Randomized EVERYTHING -New gear to aquire -A story line that doesn't force you to follow it -Base building -Ship collecting -Challenges (when sought after)  I honestly love this game and have since launch day. The reason for that is because I wasn't hyped for some overblown multiplayer space extravaganza... No, I was expecting a space game with exploration in mind and a really, really good soundtrack. Something I could come home to and relax with from a long day at work.  This game is everything I could of asked for, and now, with all the free content updates is even more than I could of ever wanted.  Keep up the good work Sean and Team at Hello Games. I salute you. *Salute*

Before you read my review, a few things: I bought this game on sale ($20 I believe), and I bought this game after all the splendid updates that improved it from the launch disaster.   That being said, I had a wonderful time playing this, as you can tell by the nearly 200 hours put into it. If you want a deep, rich story, or an action packed pace with a diversity of challenges and missions, this game will dissappoint you. I however just wanted something I could come home from work and relax to. Something I could pick up and have fun with and not add to the stress of the day. No Mans Sky was exactly that! Fun exploration, pretty darn good base and farming mechanics. Ship and freighter costs that teeter toward the edge of a grind, but are really just rewarding in nature. It has a slow start, but once you expand your crafting and purchasing power it becomes quite fun. And the fauna.. well they can be quite odd which is funny, and each planet has its own oddities. I would still be playing now if I hadnt fallen into a Witcher 3 hole as of late. But the great thing about NMS is that I can pick right up where I left off!  Review Main points: - Fun and more complete after the latest updates - For a casual exploration experience  EDIT: NEXT has really put things on track! Loads of improvements in almost every facet of the game, and they have been releasing constant updates since its launch. The development team stuck with it and have really turned things around. I cant wait to see where the No Man's Sky journey take us. Put another 100+ hours in since NEXT dropped :)

I love redemption, especially in video games. I was one of the many saps that preordered this game, and for console no less (because I had an incapable pc at the time).  I was also one of the many that rushed back to GameStop (when I still went there) to get absolutely nothing when everyone realized it was a sham and they gave nothing for the trade in (or less than usual).  I was extremely disappointed that at what seemed was going to be an adventure filled with wonder turned into a ridiculous circle of grind with no point except to get stuck in an endless circle of grind.    I bought a PC, and a few random games to mess around with to see the notable differences between console and PC, and was still seeing this game pop up in my queue.  With every update, it seemed like they were working in the right direction, but I didn't want to drop 60 bucks on it AGAIN.  When it came around to being on sale after the Atlas Update, I figured what the hell, I can drop 20 bucks on it and see what happens.  The difference between now and launch is night and day.  Yes, there are still more fixes and changes that need to be made, and that are probably already in the works.  Yes, it still needs optimizations.  But, it is SO much closer to the game that was promised to us at release.  Planets have their own personalities, their own landscapes, weather patterns, and wildlife that could be/not be a threat.  They are building on more multiplayer aspects that while still in infancy, show promise.  The development team here deserves a lot of credit for their perserverance and dedication to a game that many had written off and expected to disappear into the night.  Sitting down at a game that once bored me after 25 minutes, I find myself losing hours at a time in exploring different planets and mining materials to make products to sell to markets and find the next best ship/weapon/mining tool/blueprints/upgrade.  I'm still weary on whether or not I would pay full price on it, but the fact that I'm on the fence instead of deadset against it as I was a short time ago says something.  Just looking at the recent reviews that aren't bogged down by all the raging neckbeards with their blinders on should tell you something.  I would whole-heartedly recommend snagging this game if it is on sale, and I would recommend not taking advice from someone about this game who hasn't played it since the Atlas update, as they will probably steer you in the wrong direction.  I hope Hello Games continues to improve and keep hard at work at a game that has come MILES, against all the odds and people in the world who were very much against them.

I pre-ordred no mans sky bak in that fateful time. When the hype train was rolling at full speed and all we had was the promises of Sean Murry and a dream. Needless to say as the world soon found out that train was carrying nothing but broken dreams and regret. 10 hours in and you quickly realized there was nothing but lies and planet after planet of the same old ♥♥♥♥ with nothing very interesting to do. Quickly put it aside with the rest of the world and tossed a negative review at it.  I've come back to the game a little over a year later on a whim when I couldn't decide what I wanted to play. Not dissapointed any longer. While it is not perfect it has definitely improved and you can tell that the developers, for the most part, are listening to the community feedback and are atoning for their mistake.   There are plenty of good features to keep yuo busy in the game now if you were an original person who liked the idea and decided to pass on it at first.  There is base building now. You are limited to one planet but this base can be moved later on and you will receive a fraction of you materials back. You will also keep everything in your storage containers. There are different tiers of freighters you can buy that will offer you more storage and farming space, and the story I found pretty interesting. It's one of the first things I focused on when returning.  If you are still unwary you can always grab it on sale or from a key vendor for a lower price with not much risk. But overall its a million times better than it was at launch and worth a try.

review: At first glance...   I read the negative reviews, and saw the price tag on it, and just said "no" and moved on to another game on my wish-list. Yet overtime, on one faithful day, I saw that the No Mans's Sky was on sale. I was able to snag it for $20 or so bucks and it still is one of my favorites.   It's usually the best to play after a stressful day of in class lectures, or after a tough game of whatever fps shooter you decided to hurt yourself with. The price...can seem a little bit steep, I can understand that thought process. However, in the past, I might've agreed with waiting for a sale or finding a better deal through a CD key site. Yet as of 2020, there have been a number of DLC overhauls released (which were all free and implemented in game). Some fine examples is the Foundation Update in 2016 which brought promised features that included base building, freighters, and the new difficulty modes.  Another such DLC released is the Path Finder Update, which includes planetary vehicles, base sharing, ship and weapon specialization, perma-death mode, visual updates (higher resolution textures, HDR mode, ambient lighting, etc), being able to own multiple ships, etc etc etc.  That's not even including the Atlas update which has included a complete overhaul towards the main story, as in it gives you one to actually follow! It lets you answer questions like, "who are you?", "where are we?", "why are we here?".   In the grand scheme of things, this game is an ever growing, ever improving video game. It has done a complete 180 of launch day, and is the biggest comeback of any video game I have ever seen. This game to me is worth the price, worth the time, and worth the energy to look into.
